name: US Built Environment Quality: Street Comparisons with Strength Slider
description:
Method replication: same task, scales and design as the paper; the images are not the paper's stimuli (70 new Google Street View views from nine US metropolitan areas, one per Census division).

Larkin et al. (2025, Environmental Science & Technology) collected 72,516 Amazon Mechanical Turk surveys to train nationwide models of five built environment quality characteristics. Each survey (SI Appendix 2) has a consent form, six opt-in questions about the participant (age, gender, education, Hispanic origin, race, COVID-19 limits on going out) and six side-by-side Google Street View comparisons: which street is more safe for walking, more safe from violence or crime, has more cars (quality-assurance check), is more relaxing, is more beautiful, has a higher quality of nature. Participants pick a side with a slider and move it farther the more strongly they feel; equal is not allowed. This template keeps the questions, answer options, order and slider instructions word for word.

Data: each comparison is stored as the chosen image (pairwise choice, ranked with TrueSkill on Results) and, in slider_scores, the signed slider position (-50 left … +50 right) with the left and right image names, which is the image score the paper analysed (right image = response, left = minus response).

Differences from the original study: (1) images: the paper drew 49,440 GSV images sampled by Census division, urbanicity, road type and straight/side viewing angle, and paired them with set sampling probabilities (SI Appendix 3); here 70 views (forward, backward or side) from grids around Boston, Philadelphia, Columbus, Kansas City, Atlanta, Nashville, Dallas, Denver and Portland OR, trails and heavily blurred views removed, paired at random; (2) the consent text is shortened (no payment, contact or IRB lines); (3) "Other (specify)" for gender and race is a separate optional text box; (4) the slider range -50 to +50 follows the paper's model output range, the paper does not state the survey slider's units; (5) the COVID-19 item is kept as in the 2021–2022 survey, remove it if not relevant.

Street images: Google Street View (© Google).
